Senses.Explanation: The wild fox is anchored by Baizhang’s fox case, while separate uses name an actual fox or denounce a person as fox-like; the three referents remain distinct. A fox story becomes a named public case: the story's unnamed former abbot says that answering 'does not fall under cause and effect' brought five hundred fox births, while Baizhang Huaihai answers 'is not blind to cause and effect.' Zhenjing Kewen heads a verse simply 'Wild Fox'; Huiji Yuanxi repeatedly raises 'Baizhang's wild-fox story' in the chamber to question Daxin, and Shita Xuanmi raises the same longer title in a hall address. The abbreviated case-name is a textual object, not the animal in the story and not a person denounced as a fox.

Senses.Note: Baizhang Huaihai supplies the corpse and cremation; Fachang Yu and Hongfu Ziwen supply falling-into and escaping-from predicates; Dahui Zonggao supplies the five-hundred-birth fox. The source presents the former abbot without a personal name, so the entry invents no synthetic master identity.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names a wild fox, not the wild-fox case. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. The ordinary animal remains visible: Baizhang Huaihai leads the assembly behind the mountain, draws out a dead fox, and has it cremated. The story's unnamed former abbot says that he fell into fox births and later escaped the fox body; Fachang Yu asks why one falls into or escapes 'the fox,' Hongfu Ziwen says that understanding the paired formulas still leaves one falling into the fox, and Dahui Zonggao calls the former figure that wild fox from five hundred births ago. These named predicates still denote the animal or animal incarnation, not the name of the case and not an insult directed at a person.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names a person denounced as a wild fox, not the wild-fox case. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. A person or group is denounced as a wild fox: Zhongan Huikong says he exposes all the wild foxes under heaven, while Deshan Xuanjian coordinates people he rejects with spirits, apparitions, and wild foxes. Nanyang Huizhong's longer 'wild-fox spirit' sharpens the personal insult. Dahui Zonggao applies the still longer fox-spirit label to an understanding, but Dahui's nested compound does not make views a bare-word referent. This abusive human label is not the literal fox body or the title of the Baizhang case, and the entry does not make each named rebuke an objective verdict.

Senses.Note: The label is related by wording to the Baizhang wild-fox case (百丈野狐), but the corpus does not restrict it to citations of that case. Its verbs are openly corrective: "tear apart" (裂破), "sweep away" (掃), and "show off tricks" (逞甚伎倆). A verse placed under the Baizhang case says, "a whole troop carries on wild-fox Chan; over five hundred lives, one saying comes round" (修行一隊野狐禪，五百生來一語圓). The verse's own narrative language is retained as a recorded case allusion and not generalized beyond that witness.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 師室中常舉百丈野狐話問僧，對者多不契。一日自云：百丈野狐，野狐百丈，埋作一坑，伏惟尚享。
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source text Recorded Sayings of Xiaoyin Daxin (笑隱大訢禪師語錄): Xiaoyin Daxin is the exact speaker. The record narrates Xiaoyin Daxin’s room questioning and then explicitly marks his own words; he reverses ‘Baizhang’s wild fox’ to ‘wild-fox Baizhang’ and buries both in one pit.

Senses.Explanation: Speakers use ‘wild-fox Chan’ as an adverse label for Chan they present as counterfeit, distorted, or merely clever. The phrase can allude to the Baizhang fox case, but its attested use also ranges beyond that case as a charge against other people’s teaching or performance. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that Lia’an Qingyu, Ruibai Mingxue, Fangrong Tongxi, or another named speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Ruibai calls it "wild-fox Chan from various quarters" (諸方野狐禪) when criticizing attempts to define a lineage from Bodhidharma's reply to Emperor Wu, "really, no merit" (實無功德). Fangrong, after the cited participant shouts and then has no reply, asks, "what tricks is wild-fox Chan showing off?" (野狐禪逞甚伎倆).

Senses.Explanation: A wild-fox body is the animal body borne in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded cause-and-effect case. An old man says that his answer ‘not subject to cause and effect’ led to five hundred births in such a body; Baizhang’s ‘not blind to cause and effect’ releases him. Later monks and masters debate, question, and recast those paired formulas.
